title: Hubble’s Sweeping View of the Coma Cluster of Galaxies
caption: Part of the Coma Cluster of galaxies, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Coma Cluster, Abell 1656 · constellation Coma Berenices · about 300 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A bright spiral galaxy at upper left stands out from its neighbors, brighter and bluer than the galaxies around it, with reddish-brown dusty arms against a whiter disc. Those arms suggest it was disturbed at some point. Everything else in the frame is an elliptical, an S0 galaxy or a background galaxy lying far beyond the Coma Cluster.

The Coma Cluster, also called Abell 1656, is one of the densest known collections of galaxies. It holds thousands of them in a sphere more than 20 million light-years across, over 300 million light-years away. This section lies roughly one-third of the way out from the cluster's center.

Most galaxies in the central part of Coma are ellipticals, featureless, pale goldish-brown balls of old stars, both dwarf and giant. Spirals, with cold gas still forming new stars, sit farther out. S0 galaxies fall between the two, made of older stars with little recent star formation but with some structure such as a bar or ring.

understand.summary: A composite of exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys in yellow and near-infrared light. F475W is shown in cyan and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: About 12 hours of exposure gathered far more light than the eye can, and one filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

explore: The cluster takes its name from Coma Berenices and sits near the Milky Way's north pole, away from the dust and gas of our galaxy's plane, so it is easy to see from Earth. The data come from a Hubble survey meant to help compare galaxies in crowded and isolated settings, and nearby galaxies with more distant ones.
